extracted.intended_audience: scientists, engineers, and naturalists (readers of Nature)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating short scientific reports, letters, and reviews across multiple disciplines (physics spectroscopy, metallurgy/corrosion, meteorology, natural history, museum curation) as published in a general science journal. Focuses on assessing experimental design, observational completeness, theoretical–observational comparison, and presentation/recognition standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical–observational frequency matching (secondary hydrogen spectrum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare calculated spectral frequencies with observed secondary hydrogen lines and accept matches when agreement lies within an absolute error of one unit of frequency; use integral quantum numbers over specified ranges and standard reference values for observed frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the reported work 47 lines agreed with calculated values within an absolute error of one unit of frequency, taking integral values of m and n from r up to 10, values of m3 from 1 to 15, and x3 taken as 2 and 3. The values obtained by Merton and Barratt (Phil. Trans. A, 1922, pp. 388-400) were employed as the standard of reference. Present matches in a table showing formula, calculated, observed, error, and line character/intensity; look for grouping/series behaviour according to the quantum numbers and note physical similarities among series. Interpret matched frequencies (where appropriate) as 'summation tones' (sum of a Balmer or Paschen frequency and an infrared frequency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement and justification of theoretical assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the assumptions and modifications of the theoretical model explicit (e.g., charge values, electron arrangement, mass corrections) and justify any parameter corrections when adapting solutions from related systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author adapted Silberstein's solution for neutral helium to negatively charged hydrogen by changing the charge (E instead of 2E) and replacing 4N by N, and made a correction to N to account for two electrons changing the electron-mass correction for finite nuclear mass. It was assumed as a first approximation that electrons are arranged antipodally so forces are central. State such assumptions clearly and note their possible limitations when comparing to observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative reference data for observational standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing theoretical predictions to observed data, use published, authoritative reference values as the standard of comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merton and Barratt's tabulated values were used as the standard of reference for observed hydrogen frequencies. Cite the reference used and, where possible, use the most recent, critically evaluated data sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational reporting checklist for winter thunderstorms
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and report a standard set of observational details for each thunderstorm occurrence to ensure usefulness for climatological study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requested 'chief points' to be recorded: times at which storms occur (especially times of passage overhead), whether storm was severe or only one/two flashes or claps, any change of wind or drop of temperature with the storm, whether there was rain, hail, or snow, direction of lightning when seen at night, and any other potentially interesting information. Reports should note location (with emphasis on under-sampled regions) and be submitted by postcard or letter to the investigator. This forms a minimum standardized dataset for winter thunderstorm compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of test materials and specimen preparation for corrosion exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a representative set of materials and prepare specimens in dimensions and surface condition that reflect practical/constructive use to obtain realistic corrosion-resistance data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee exposed fourteen types of ferrous material including various irons and steels; specimens were rolled plates 24 in × 3 in × 0.5 in (cast irons prepared by casting). In general specimens retained their outer skin of oxide to resemble service conditions; in two cases oxide was removed to test effect. Avoid excessive laboratory-only conditioning unless representing a deliberate variable; include at least one heat-treated specimen to represent 'optimum' condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical testing protocol accompanying corrosion studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a suite of mechanical tests (shock, hardness, tensile) on both treated and untreated specimens, with attention to sampling along bars to detect strain effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Izod and Frémont shock tests and Brinell hardness tests; carry out tensile tests on bars marked at regular intervals to measure elongation point-to-point. Prepare duplicate tensile bars for immersion so that post-exposure mechanical changes can be assessed. Plan to cut small test pieces from differently strained parts for laboratory corrosion tests to correlate mechanical strain with corrosibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microstructural and chemical analyses as corrosion predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct chemical analyses and photomicrographic studies of treated and untreated specimens and correlate microstructure (grain size, ferrite/pearlite distribution) with corrosion and mechanical properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photomicrographs: longitudinal sections at ~100× for grain elongation and transverse sections at ~600× for microstructure. Record grain counts where relevant (example: grains per square inch increased markedly with heat treatment). Correlate microstructure changes (e.g., reduced grain size, more homogeneous structure) with improved shock and corrosion performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field exposure regimes and site replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose replicated specimen sets under multiple realistic environmental regimes at several locations to distinguish immersion, tidal, and atmospheric corrosion effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each location (Plymouth, Auckland, Colombo, Halifax) expose one set completely immersed, one at half-tide level (alternately wet and dry), and one to sea air only. Keep precise records of specimen positions in mounting frames; weigh specimens before exposure; pack and ship to minimize identity loss; design marking robust to severe corrosion (e.g., drilled holes encoding classification letter and bar number preserved by surrounding concrete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls for specimen identity and data integrity under severe corrosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt marking and mounting methods that preserve specimen identification even after severe corrosion or possible physical loss from frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drilled-hole coding at both ends of plates where holes are preserved inside concrete embedments: one end encodes classification letter (type of metal) and the other encodes the bar number. Keep a precise record of each specimen's position in the frame to guard against mixing; design frames to prevent fall-out of badly corroded bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of strain and contact-with-dissimilar-metals as experimental variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally include specimens that simulate strain and contact conditions expected in service (bent bars, rivetted/bolted connections, dissimilar-metal contact) to study their effect on corrosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a few bars bent at right angles, others fitted with ordinary rivets and bolts, and some bolted together. These simulate real-world assemblies and allow assessment of galvanic and strain-related corrosion phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heat treatment as an independent test variable and its characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Include heat-treated specimens to represent 'optimal' material conditions and report the quantitative improvements in mechanical properties and microstructure produced by treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example results: for mild steel heat treatment raised yield point, maximum stress, and Brinell hardness numbers substantially and increased grain homogeneity (e.g., grains per square inch from 820,000 to ~5,000,000). Document heat-treatment procedures and compare treated vs untreated in corrosion and mechanical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of functional properties alongside corrosion resistance (case: hydrophone diaphragms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing materials for service parts, evaluate both corrosion resistance and relevant functional properties (e.g., acoustic behaviour) and note trade-offs between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During wartime tests, nickel steel resisted corrosion well but had inferior acoustic properties compared with chromium (stainless) steel, which combined corrosion resistance with superior elastic limit and hardness. Also inspect for manufacturing defects (e.g., over-heating causing coarse grain), and demonstrate that remedial heat-treatment can restore corrosion resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for museum exhibition and public-education presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt exhibit-layout principles and educational services aimed at accurate, instructive displays: choose faunistic/geographical organization when appropriate, display animals in associated natural groups, and support school education services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The American Museum emphasizes a faunistic/geographical basis and displays animals in associated groups under natural conditions (e.g., African elephant group). Plan building space and endowment to support large faunistic displays; consider dedicated school service buildings and international cooperation for specimen collection and exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for scholarly recognition and presentation of honours
rubrics_metrics.description: For institutional presentations to distinguished scientists, choose durable, artistic tokens (plaques, medal replicas) with clear inscriptions and involve peers/contributors in subscription and ceremony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suggested presentation to Sir Edward Sharpey Schafer took the form of a full-sized plaque with medal replicas for subscribers; the medal bears an inscription and the bronze plaque mounted on stone. Engage former demonstrators and colleagues; ensure high artistic quality and good portrait likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of independent confirmation for establishing observational claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Give weight to independent, concordant observations as evidence to overturn traditional misconceptions in natural-history and field observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: independent observations confirming Sinel's earlier report on the natural position of the anemone on hermit-crabs help to oppose a traditional but incorrect textbook depiction. Note provenance and priority claims where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and practical importance argumentation in scientific reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing applied subjects (e.g., corrosion), quantify or estimate economic impact and argue for practical research directions (e.g., development of alloy steels) even when precise statistics are unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Robert Hadfield estimated annual wastage due to rusting well over £700 million (including galvanizing, painting costs). Use such estimates to justify research programmes and industrial adoption of corrosion-resistant alloys, while acknowledging limitations of the statistics.
